findings.summary: FORTERRA ACQUISITION OF GOTENNA (Oct 2025): Forterra acquired goTenna, a tactical mesh networking company, for undisclosed price (Barclays advised goTenna). goTenna's decentralized communications technology adds comms capability to Forterra's autonomous platforms in GPS-denied and comms-contested environments. This is a vertical integration play — autonomous vehicles need reliable C2 links, and goTenna provides mesh networking independent of traditional infrastructure. Combined with AutoDrive autonomy and the Arlington VA office (opened Feb 2026), Forterra is assembling a full-stack autonomous military ground vehicle company: perception + autonomy + communications + government affairs.

curation.lead:
Forterra, legally registered as Robotic Research Opco, LLC, is an autonomous military ground vehicle company headquartered in Clarksburg, Maryland [Finding #6796]. Founded in 2002 by Alberto Lacaze and Karl Murphy — both former researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology — the company operated for nineteen years as a bootstrapped SBIR/STTR contractor before raising $228 million in a Series A round led by SoftBank Vision Fund 2 in December 2021 [Finding #6799]. The company rebranded from Robotic Research to Forterra in February 2024 and reached a valuation exceeding $1 billion after closing a $238 million Series C round led by Moore Strategic Ventures in November 2025 [Finding #6799]. Total venture funding stands at approximately $541 million.

Forterra develops the AutoDrive autonomous navigation system, which has been integrated across twelve or more military vehicle platforms. The company holds an estimated $380 million in identified federal contract value [Finding #6801], including a $114 million prime contract for autonomous breaching systems fielded with the Army's 27th Engineer Battalion, production contracts for the Marine Corps' ROGUE-Fires autonomous missile launcher under the NMESIS program (with Oshkosh Defense as prime contractor), and prototype work on autonomous armored vehicles with BAE Systems and autonomous precision fires launchers with RTX [Finding #6802]. Forterra claims to be the only company competing across all four Department of Defense ground autonomy programs. In October 2025, Forterra acquired goTenna, a tactical mesh networking company that holds a $99 million IDIQ contract with U.S. Customs and Border Protection [Finding #6800].

The company's investor base spans two distinct networks: the traditional Washington defense establishment, represented by Enlightenment Capital (whose advisory board includes former Deputy Secretary of Defense Bob Work, former Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General James Cartwright, and former Secretary of the Air Force Deborah Lee James) [Finding #6809], and Silicon Valley defense technology capital, including SoftBank, RTX Ventures, Hanwha Asset Management, and NightDragon [Finding #6808]. Forterra's senior leadership includes six officials with direct government-to-contractor career paths [Finding #6806], and the company operates a political action committee that has directed donations to members of the House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee and the House Armed Services Committee [Finding #6813]. Congress added $30 million above the Pentagon's own request for ROGUE-Fires autonomy kits in the FY2026 defense budget, a line item that aligns with Forterra's disclosed lobbying on the relevant appropriations bills [Finding #6812].
curation.system_role: A twenty-year SBIR-incubated robotics company that transitioned to venture-backed defense contractor status, bridging the traditional Pentagon procurement establishment and the Silicon Valley defense technology ecosystem through parallel investor networks and systematic personnel recruitment from government, military, and competitor organizations.

sections.title: Corporate Identity and Evolution
sections.content:
The entity now known as Forterra was incorporated in Delaware on September 13, 2002, as Robotic Research LLC [Finding #6796]. Its founders, Alberto Lacaze and Karl Murphy, had both served as technical leads at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, where they worked on the Demo I through Demo III autonomous vehicle programs — federally funded research initiatives that laid the groundwork for military ground autonomy [Finding #6806]. The company registered with SAM.gov under UEI VNUQN3KJKPV4 and CAGE code 3BZU0, with primary NAICS codes in search, detection, and navigation systems (334511), motor vehicle electronic equipment (336320), and physical sciences R&D (541715) [Finding #6796].

For its first nineteen years, Robotic Research operated without outside investment, building its technology base through Army SBIR and STTR contracts. USASpending records show $67.5 million in direct federal obligations from FY2008 through FY2026, with $64 million from the Department of Defense, $3.3 million from the Department of Homeland Security, and $296,000 from the Department of the Interior [Finding #6797]. The company's SBIR portfolio on SBIR.gov lists 77 awards (53 Phase I, 24 Phase II) totaling $27.4 million [Finding #6801]. This R&D work produced the AutoDrive autonomous navigation platform, which became the company's core commercial product.

The company rebranded as Robotic Research Autonomous Industries (RRAI) before adopting the name Forterra in February 2024, combining "for" and the Latin "terra" while retaining the double-R of Robotic Research [Finding #6796]. The February 2026 opening of an Arlington, Virginia office near the Pentagon marked the company's transition toward a Washington-facing posture [Finding #6796]. As of late 2025, Forterra employed between 450 and 600 people across offices in Clarksburg, Arlington, Winter Park (Florida), Ketchum (Idaho), and Palo Alto (California) [Finding #6796].

sections.title: Defense Program Integration
sections.content:
Forterra maintains active positions across eight Department of Defense programs spanning three military services [Finding #6802]. The company's $114 million prime contract for autonomous breaching systems, deployed with the Army's 27th Engineer Battalion at the Joint Readiness Training Center, represents both the largest single identified contract and the deepest operational integration — these systems are reported to be in active combat use for mine-clearing operations [Finding #6801][Finding #6802].

The Marine Corps' ROGUE-Fires program — the Remotely Operated Ground Unit for Expeditionary Fires — constitutes the Department of Defense's first production contract for ground vehicle autonomy [Finding #6802]. Under this program, Forterra provides the AutoDrive autonomous navigation system as a subcontractor to Oshkosh Defense, which builds the JLTV-based launcher that carries Naval Strike Missiles as part of the Navy Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS). Production began in mid-2025, with 48 vehicles planned for delivery. Congress appropriated $59 million for ROGUE-Fires autonomy kits in FY2026, $30 million above the Pentagon's own request [Finding #6804]. However, the Marine Corps awarded Kodiak AI a parallel autonomy contract for ROGUE-Fires in January 2026, indicating deliberate maintenance of competitive alternatives [Finding #6802].

In partnership with RTX (Raytheon) and Oshkosh Defense, Forterra demonstrated the DeepFires autonomous launcher prototypes at Project Convergence 2025 — a live-fire exercise validating autonomous Tomahawk and PAC-3 launcher concepts feeding into the Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) program [Finding #6802]. The BAE Systems partnership announced in April 2025 targets autonomous operation of the Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle, a platform with an estimated $20 billion total program value already fielding to Armored Brigade Combat Teams [Finding #6802]. Additional programs include the ATV-S/GEARS autonomous logistics truck effort (a winner-take-all downselect against Carnegie Robotics expected mid-FY2026), the UxS Autonomy program for unmanned tactical squad vehicles, and a voice-commanded autonomy SBIR adjacent to the Army's XM30 infantry fighting vehicle [Finding #6802].

Cross-referencing the company's contract history reveals a pattern: a $49.7 million Expedient Leader Follower contract awarded in June 2018 for autonomous convoy kits on Oshkosh PLS trucks was closed in 2023 without fielding operational systems [Finding #6801]. The GEARS/ATV-S program addresses the same PLS platform and mission set, representing a second attempt at autonomous logistics convoys after the first program's termination.

sections.title: Investor Network Architecture
sections.content:
Forterra's capital structure reflects investment from two distinct networks that rarely overlap in defense procurement [Finding #6810]. The first is the traditional Washington defense establishment. Enlightenment Capital, a Chevy Chase, Maryland-based private equity firm founded by Devin Talbott (whose career path ran through Lazard, the Carlyle Group, and TCG Financial Partners — the merchant bank of former Secretary of Defense William Cohen), has invested across the Series A, B, and C rounds [Finding #6809]. Enlightenment Capital's advisory board includes former Deputy Secretary of Defense Bob Work (2014–2017), who architected the Third Offset Strategy that established autonomous systems as a Pentagon priority; former Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General James Cartwright; former Secretary of the Air Force Deborah Lee James; and former Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics Ken Krieg [Finding #6809]. The fund manages $825 million in its fifth fund and oversees 42 portfolio companies generating $1.9 billion in combined revenue [Finding #6809].

The second network centers on Moore Strategic Ventures, the personal investment vehicle of Louis Moore Bacon, founder of Moore Capital Management [Finding #6811]. Moore Capital, formerly a $40 billion-plus global macro hedge fund, returned $8.9 billion to outside investors in November 2019 and converted to a proprietary fund. Moore Strategic Ventures led both Forterra's Series B ($75 million, September 2024) and Series C ($238 million, November 2025), committing over $300 million of Bacon's personal capital [Finding #6811]. As a single-LP family office vehicle operating without fund lifecycle constraints, Moore Strategic can sustain concentrated positions that traditional venture funds cannot. The fund has built a deliberate defense technology cluster including Second Front Systems (defense DevSecOps, founded by former Marines), Adarga (UK defense AI), and Paramify (FedRAMP compliance) [Finding #6811].

RTX Ventures, the corporate venture arm of RTX (Raytheon), invested in the Series C while simultaneously serving as Forterra's partner on the DeepFires autonomous launcher program [Finding #6808][Finding #6799]. Hanwha Asset Management, representing South Korea's largest defense conglomerate (manufacturer of the K9 howitzer, rocket systems, and armored vehicles), also entered at the Series C [Finding #6808]. NightDragon, the cybersecurity and defense fund of Dave DeWalt — who served on the National Security Telecommunications Advisory Committee across four presidential administrations and advises the Army Cyber Institute — participated in the same round [Finding #6808]. Ross Fubini of XYZ Venture Capital, a defense technology-focused fund, holds a Forterra board seat [Finding #6808]. SoftBank Vision Fund 2 led the $228 million Series A in December 2021 but did not participate in subsequent rounds [Finding #6799].

sections.title: Personnel Transitions
sections.content:
Six Forterra senior officials followed direct government-to-contractor career paths [Finding #6806]. Ari Schuler, who serves as president of Forterra's goTenna division, created Customs and Border Protection's innovation program while serving as a DHS official. He subsequently became CEO of goTenna, which won a $99 million IDIQ contract with CBP — the agency whose innovation capabilities he had developed. Forterra acquired goTenna in October 2025, and Schuler now leads that business unit [Finding #6805].

Stephen Rubright, Forterra's Head of Government Affairs and PAC treasurer, graduated from West Point, served in combat with the XVIII Airborne Corps during Operation Iraqi Freedom (2005–2006), then served as a Military Legislative Assistant to Senator Kay Bailey Hutchison and Representative Jeff Miller — the latter of whom chaired the House Armed Services Committee from 2015 to 2016 [Finding #6814]. Rubright subsequently worked as the Army's Senior Legislative Strategist on its appropriations liaison team before entering the private sector as a lobbyist at Astellas Pharma and then joining Forterra in May 2025 [Finding #6814]. He is affiliated with the Center for a New American Security [Finding #6814].

Sarah Flaim, Head of Congressional Affairs, previously served on the staff of the House Appropriations Committee and the House Financial Services Committee before becoming a Managing Director at DCI Group, a lobbying and public relations firm [Finding #6806]. Kevin Turner, the Chief Legal Officer who joined in October 2025, served as General Counsel at three federal agencies — the Development Finance Corporation, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, and the Export-Import Bank — and as Chief of Staff to U.S. Senator Luther Strange of Alabama [Finding #6806].

The company's operational leadership draws from a connected network of defense technology startups. Chief Growth Officer Scott Sanders served as a MARSOC special operations team leader, then held senior business development roles at Anduril Industries (where he built a $1 billion SOCOM acquisition strategy) and Vannevar Labs before joining Forterra [Finding #6798]. Chief Innovation Officer Scott Philips worked as an early forward-deployed engineer at Palantir Technologies, then served as CTO of Vannevar Labs before joining Forterra in October 2025 [Finding #6808]. CEO Josh Araujo is a retired Marine officer who worked in defense investment banking at Jefferies before joining as COO in 2021 [Finding #6798]. COO Colin Chisholm served fifteen years in the Marine Corps; VP of Defense Business Development Patrick Acox is a Marine Corps reservist [Finding #6798].

sections.title: Political Activity and Lobbying
sections.content:
Forterra registered a political action committee — the Robotic Research OpCo LLC - Forterra Political Action Committee [FEC:C00905505] — on May 16, 2025, designated as a Lobbyist/Registrant PAC [Finding #6812]. Through December 31, 2025, the PAC raised $33,082 from company executives, with Alberto Lacaze (founder, $5,000), Joseph Putney (CTO, $5,000), Stephen Rubright ($4,900), and Ari Schuler ($2,950) as the largest contributors [Finding #6807].

PAC disbursements targeted three officeholders: $1,000 to Representative Andrew Garbarino (R-NY), Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee; $500 to Senator Mark Warner (D-VA), Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee; and $500 to Representative Johnny Olszewski (D-MD), a Maryland member adjacent to Forterra's headquarters district [Finding #6813]. Personal donations from executives followed a dual-track pattern: Rubright directed contributions to House Armed Services Committee members — Representative Rich McCormick (R-GA, $500; serves on the Cyber, IT, and Innovation subcommittee with direct jurisdiction over ground autonomy programs), Representative Pat Harrigan (R-NC, $500; West Point graduate), and Representative John McGuire (R-VA, $500) [Finding #6813]. CEO Araujo directed contributions to Appropriations Committee members — Representative John Carter (R-TX, $3,500; Defense Subcommittee, Army Caucus co-chair) and Representative Tom Cole (R-OK, $600; Chairman of the House Appropriations Committee) [Finding #6813].

Forterra's lobbying expenditures rose from $10,000 in 2021 to $130,000 in 2024 and $305,000 in 2025 [Finding #6812]. LD-2 disclosure filings identify lobbying on H.R. 8070 and S.4638 (National Defense Authorization Act: autonomous driving systems acquisition and commercial autonomy policy) and H.R. 8774 and S.4921 (Defense Appropriations: funding for Army and Marine Corps autonomous ground vehicles) [Finding #6812]. The FY2026 defense appropriations bill ultimately included $59 million for ROGUE-Fires autonomy kits — $30 million above the Department of Defense's own budget request — in a program where Forterra serves as the primary autonomy provider [Finding #6804].

sections.title: Competitive Position
sections.content:
Analysis of Forterra's defense program portfolio indicates high and accelerating institutional integration that has not yet reached irreplaceability [Finding #6803]. The company has crossed the critical threshold from R&D into production on ROGUE-Fires, operates across three military service branches, and serves as the preferred autonomy integrator for both Oshkosh Defense (the Department of Defense's primary tactical vehicle manufacturer) and BAE Systems (the Army's tracked vehicle prime). The goTenna acquisition added organic communications capability, integrating mesh networking with the autonomy layer [Finding #6800].

Competitive pressure persists across multiple programs. Kodiak AI (NASDAQ: KDK) won a parallel Marine Corps contract for ROGUE-Fires autonomy in January 2026, demonstrating that Forterra does not hold sole-source status on its flagship program [Finding #6802]. The ATV-S/GEARS program is structured as a winner-take-all downselect against Carnegie Robotics at mid-FY2026 [Finding #6803]. Overland AI, backed by Anduril Industries, competes on the UxS autonomy and breaching programs. Applied Intuition, valued at $15 billion, represents a potential future competitor in defense autonomy software [Finding #6803]. An Army restructuring of ground vehicle autonomy programs in December 2025 introduced additional budget uncertainty [Finding #6803].

Forterra's structural position as a software and integration layer — rather than a vehicle manufacturer — creates both opportunity and vulnerability. The company can partner with multiple prime contractors simultaneously (Oshkosh, BAE, RTX), but it depends on those primes for hardware platforms. If a prime contractor chose to develop or acquire its own autonomy capability, Forterra's position on that platform would be at risk [Finding #6803].
